item.title: Kumano Hongu Taisha: Head Shrine of the Kumano Faith — Guide
item.description: Kumano Hongu Taisha is the head shrine of the some 3,000 Kumano shrines across Japan and the spiritual heart of the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage, the destination toward which most pilgrims walked. Reached by a stone stairway lined with banners, its cypress-bark-roofed halls stand in dignified, unpainted simplicity beneath tall cedars. A short walk away lies Oyunohara, the shrine’s original site on a river sandbank until a flood destroyed it in 1889, now an empty sacred field approached through the largest torii gate in the world — a colossal steel arch 34 metres high, standing starkly against the sky.

item.title: Kashihara Jingu: Shrine of Japan's First Emperor — Guide
item.description: Kashihara Jingu, at the foot of Mount Unebi in southern Nara, is one of Japan’s most important modern shrines, built in 1890 on the legendary spot where, according to myth, Emperor Jimmu — the first emperor of Japan — acceded to the throne and founded the nation in 660 BC. Its grand halls of unpainted hinoki cypress, some relocated from the Kyoto Imperial Palace, stand within vast, serene wooded grounds designed as a national sanctuary.
